title: Integrating bioinformatics, molecular dynamics simulation and experimental verification to screen diagnostic biomarkers for polyamine metabolism-related osteoarthritis and predict potential drugs
journal: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research

sections.abstract:
Osteoarthritis (OA) represents a prevalent chronic joint degeneration disorder regulated by multiple factors. Polyamine metabolism (PM) contributes substantially to OA development. However, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. The current study aimed to identify PM-related OA biomarkers and to discover potential therapeutic small-molecule compounds (SMCs). The goal was to lay the groundwork for future diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for OA.

The current study screened differentially expressed PM-related genes (DEPMGs) by integrating data from the Gene Expression Omnibus and GeneCards databases. Next, functional annotations were performed for Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was used to pinpoint crucial modular genes. Then, four machine learning algorithms were employed to determine the hub genes. Their diagnostic efficacy was evaluated via nomogram models and receiver operating characteristic curves. We screened SMCs with potential for treating OA through molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. Finally, to validate the expression of the aforementioned biomarkers, qRT-PCR and Western blot experiments were performed in a hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 )-treated C-28/I2 human chondrocyte model.

First, thirty DEPMGs were screened. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed their involvement in biological processes, including the cellular response to lipopolysaccharide, chondrogenesis, and the IL-17 signaling pathway. Using WGCNA and machine learning, four hub genes were identified. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that triptolide exhibited a strong binding affinity with the target protein and that the binding system demonstrated excellent stability. In vitro experiments revealed that the four hub genes were significantly upregulated in OA ( p < 0.05), consistent with the bioinformatics predictions.

This study initially identified four genes closely associated with polyamine metabolism-related genes: PLOD1, TSPO, SPP1, and COL6A1. These genes demonstrated potential value in the early diagnosis and precise intervention of OA. Triptolide was also found to have therapeutic potential for treating OA. These findings lay the groundwork for developing OA biomarkers and innovative therapeutic strategies.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s13018-025-06544-y.
sections.introduction:
Osteoarthritis (OA) constitutes a prevalent chronic joint degeneration disorder. The Global Burden of Disease study estimates that around 600 million individuals worldwide are affected, with a higher prevalence observed in females [ 1 ]. OA’s onset is associated with factors such as age, obesity, trauma, and genetics [ 2 ]. The pathological characteristics mainly include articular cartilage erosion, synovitis, and subchondral sclerosis accompanied by osteophyte formation [ 3 , 4 ]. These factors can lead to clinical manifestations such as joint pain, deformity, and functional limitations [ 3 ]. Current treatment approaches primarily involve medication, physical therapy, and joint replacement surgery. These approaches can alleviate symptoms to some extent, but they have yet to achieve ideal overall efficacy. While significant progress has been made in recent years in the development of early identification technologies and targeted intervention strategies, establishing a causative treatment system for OA and refining widely accessible ultra-early diagnosis protocols still require further exploration and advancement [ 5 , 6 ].

Polyamines (PAs) are a class of small-molecule cationic compounds widely present in eukaryotes [ 7 ]. They mainly include putrescine, spermidine, and spermine. Their metabolism is regulated by synthetic enzymes, catabolic enzymes, and transport proteins [ 7 ]. PAs participate in many fundamental processes of cell growth and development. These processes include maintaining protein and nucleic acid synthesis, stabilizing chromatin structure, and regulating cell differentiation and apoptosis [ 8 , 9 ]. PAs also contribute to resistance against oxidative damage and nucleic acid depurination and modulate various ion channels necessary for intercellular communication [ 10 ]. Numerous studies have indicated a close and complex relationship between polyamine metabolism (PM) and various diseases, particularly tumors and nervous system disorders [ 11 , 12 ]. In recent years, their potential role in OA has also gradually attracted attention. Progressive degradation and destruction of the chondrocyte extracellular matrix (ECM) is the most important pathological feature of OA [ 3 ]. Research has demonstrated that PA synthesis is critically involved in S -adenosylmethionine-induced ECM production [ 13 , 14 ]. Furthermore, Ou et al. have found that spermidine can improve the degeneration of articular cartilage by regulating the M1/M2 polarization state of synovial macrophages [ 15 ]. Guo et al. have discovered that spermidine demonstrates anti-inflammatory and anti-pyroptotic effects in chondrocytes by modulating both the AhR/NF-κB signaling axis and the NLRP3/caspase-1/GSDMD cascade [ 16 ]. PAs may also activate autophagy and promote chondrogenesis by increasing the expression of acetyltransferase EP300 [ 17 ]. Due to the current limited understanding of the interplay between PM and OA pathogenesis and the lack of clinically available OA diagnostic biomarkers derived from PM pathways, a comprehensive and systematic analysis of polyamine metabolism-related genes (PMGs) is particularly necessary.

Based on the aforementioned background, the current study analyzed OA-related expression profiles from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, as well as PMGs retrieved from GeneCards. Differentially expressed PMGs (DEPMGs) were screened. Hub genes were identified via machine learning (ML) methods and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Subsequently, in vitro validation was performed through quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and Western blot. Furthermore, the study also screened potential small-molecule compounds (SMCs) targeting OA. With the help of molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation techniques, it analyzed the binding ability and stability between these compounds and target proteins. It is hoped to explore the role of PMGs in the pathogenesis of OA and evaluate its potential as a diagnostic marker and therapeutic target. This will provide a new theoretical basis and practical guidance for early diagnosis and precise treatment of OA.
sections.methods:
Gene expression profiles from four datasets ( GSE55235 , GSE57218 , GSE82107 , and GSE55457 ) were retrieved from the GEO database ( http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ). Table 1 summarizes their basic characteristics. Due to the lack of clinical metadata (such as age, gender, and disease severity) in some datasets, the relevant metadata were not listed in the table. GSE55235 , GSE57218 , and GSE82107 were designated as the training set for subsequent model development. GSE55457 served as the validation set. The raw data of gene expression profiles were read and preprocessed via R software (version 4.4.2). The aforementioned datasets were normalized using the “limma” R package, and the training set was combined. Then, the batch effect was corrected utilizing the “sva” R package, and the final gene expression matrix was obtained. Furthermore, 919 PMGs were retrieved from the GeneCards database ( https://www.genecards.org/ ). The analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was performed via the ‘limma’ package in R software. The screening criteria were set as |log2(fold change)|≥ 0.585 and FDR < 0.05. Additionally, heatmaps and volcano plots of DEGs were generated via the “pheatmap” and “ggplot2” packages in R software. The intersection of DEGs and 919 PMGs was taken to obtain DEPMGs.

An expression enrichment analysis was carried out on DEPMGs. This comprised Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis and Gene Ontology (GO) functional annotation across all three sub-ontologies (molecular function [MF], cellular component [CC], and biological process [BP]). These analyses aimed to uncover important biological pathways connected to DEPMGs and obtain functional annotation information. The enrichment analysis was completed via the Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID, https://david.ncifcrf.gov/ ). The analysis results were visualized through the “ggplot2” package in R software.

To investigate the interaction relationship between DEPMGs, PPI data were extracted from the String database ( http://string-db.org/ ) to construct the interaction network. Subsequently, the PPI network was visualized using the open-source bioinformatics software Cytoscape to present the molecular interaction network characteristics intuitively.

This study utilized the “WGCNA” R package to select the top 3000 genes with the highest variance in expression data for preprocessing. Abnormal samples were excluded via cluster analysis, and a gene pair correlation matrix was calculated to generate a similarity matrix. Based on the characteristics of scale-free network topology, a soft threshold of β = 5 was selected, and the similarity matrix was transformed into an adjacency matrix to strengthen the strong association between genes. The correlation between module feature vectors and target features was evaluated. After merging similar modules, we calculated the correlation coefficients between each module eigengene (ME) and the target trait, as well as the proportion of variance explained by each ME. We prioritized modules with high correlation for screening key module genes.

Intersection analysis of DEPMGs and key module genes yielded candidate genes. The Spearman correlation matrix between genes was calculated using the “linkET” package and visualized through qcorrplot.

This study implemented the LASSO algorithm using the “glmnet” package in R for L1-regularized modeling of the gene expression matrix. The cv.glmnet function was applied for fivefold cross-validation to determine the optimal regularization parameter (λ_(min)) and extract genes with non-zero coefficients. Next, we utilized the SVM-RFE algorithm from the caret package, using a radial basis kernel function for recursive feature elimination. Ten-fold cross-validation automatically identified the optimal subset that minimized root mean square error (RMSE) while preventing information leakage from the training set. Additionally, a random forest model comprising 1000 decision trees was constructed using the “randomForest” package. The optimal number of trees was determined by analyzing the out-of-bag (OOB) error curve. Genes with a mean decrease in Gini index greater than one were selected based on their importance scores. Furthermore, the association between each gene and grouping was analyzed by univariate logistic regression (glm function). Features with significance thresholds below 0.05 were retained. A forest plot was drawn. The odds ratio (OR) and confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Finally, the “ggvenn” package was applied to create a Venn diagram to extract the intersection of features selected by the four methods, forming a high-specificity candidate marker set.

Based on this model, we employed the nomogram function from the “rms” package to construct a nomogram. The total score was mapped to a predictive probability axis to intuitively visualize disease risk. Subsequently, calibration curves were generated to assess the agreement between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes. Decision curve analysis (DCA) was also performed to evaluate the model's net benefit in clinical decision-making. To comprehensively assess the diagnostic performance, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was conducted, and the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated. Additionally, Bootstrap resampling is employed for internal validation. 1000 samples are drawn with replacement from the original training set, and after refitting the model each time, the AUC is calculated on the original dataset. Finally, the average value of the 1000 AUC results is taken. Additionally, an external dataset was used to validate the robustness and reliability of the model. Finally, differential expression patterns were visualized using boxplots generated via the “ggpubr” package.

The CIBERSORT algorithm was utilized to determine the infiltration proportions of 22 human immune cell types in the training dataset samples. Further analysis included investigating correlations between immune cell infiltration and hub gene expression. It also explored the expression patterns of immune checkpoint genes and evaluated their relationship with the overall gene expression profile.

We used the online analysis platform NetworkAnalyst ( https://www.networkanalyst.ca ), which integrates resources from the JASPER and mirTarbase databases. We employed this platform to systematically predict the binding sites and potential interactions between transcription factors (TFs) and microRNAs (miRNAs) with target biomarkers. The predicted data were then imported into Cytoscape visualization software to construct TF-gene and gene-miRNA regulatory network maps, thereby visually presenting the regulatory associations at different molecular levels.

The Connectivity Map (CMap) database ( https://cmap.ihmc.us/ ) predicts drugs based on differential gene expression. It analyzes functional associations between genes, SMCs, and diseases. The top 150 upregulated and downregulated genes from the OA differential gene profile were submitted to the CMap database, and their expression patterns were compared with those induced by existing SMCs on the platform. A correlation score ranging from − 100 to 100 was generated. The database returned a list of compounds that exhibited strong correlations with the query gene set. A positive score indicates a positive correlation between the input gene expression profile and the reference profile, while a negative score reflects an inverse correlation. Generally, the more negative the correlation score, the stronger the potential for the compound to reverse the disease-associated gene expression pattern, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic agent. Ultimately, the ten SMCs with the most negative enrichment scores were selected for further investigation.

To verify the binding ability of the candidate compound to the key protein, protein–ligand docking studies were performed. The 3D structure of the target protein was downloaded from the AlphaFold database ( https://alphafold.com/ ) and saved in PDB format. CMAP-predicted small molecules (PubChem SDF files) were converted to mol2 format using OpenBabel. Subsequently, AutoDock was employed for molecular docking to calculate the binding energy between the protein receptor and small-molecule ligand, with a docking score of ≤ − 5.0 kcal/mol generally recognized as an indicator of strong interaction. Finally, docking results were visualized through PyMOL software ( http://www.pymol.org ) to analyze the interaction modes between compounds and target proteins intuitively.

Molecular dynamics simulations were performed using GROMACS 2022. The force field parameters for the receptor protein and ligand were assigned using the AMBER14SB and GAFF2 force fields, respectively. This was done with the pdb2gmx tool and the AutoFF web server. The system was solvated in a cubic TIP3P water box with an edge length of 1 nm [ 18 ]. Counterions were added using gmx genion to maintain overall charge neutrality. Long-range electrostatic interactions were treated using the Particle-Mesh Ewald (PME) method with a cutoff of 1 nm. All covalent bonds were constrained using the SHAKE algorithm, and integration was carried out with the Verlet leapfrog algorithm at a time step of 1 fs. Before the production simulation, the system underwent two steps of energy minimization. First, 3000 steepest descent steps were performed to quickly eliminate unfavorable contacts. Then, fine-tuning was conducted using the conjugate gradient method over 2000 steps. The simulation was conducted under NPT ensemble conditions at 310 K for 100 ns. After the simulation, built-in tools in GROMACS were used to analyze the trajectories. By calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD), root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), hydrogen bonds (HBonds), radius of gyration (Rg), and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), the stability and dynamic characteristics of the system were evaluated.

The C-28/I2 chondrocyte cell line, provided by Cloud-Clone Corp., was used. As a human-derived cell line, the C-28/I2 can simulate the characteristics of primary chondrocytes. It has been widely used in in vitro experiments that require a large number of cells for the study of reproducible models of chondrocyte physiology and pathology. In the experiments, C-28/I2 chondrocytes were cultured in DMEM medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum. Normal chondrocytes were successfully induced into an OA cell model by adding 100 μM H 2 O 2 and incubating for 24 h at 37 °C in a 5% CO 2 atmosphere [ 19 ].

Total RNA was extracted from cells using TRIpure Total RNA Extraction Reagent (ELK Biotechnology, EP013) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Subsequently, cDNA reverse transcription was performed using the EntiLink™ 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (ELK Biotechnology, EQ003). Afterwards, qPCR was performed on a StepOne™ Real-Time PCR instrument (Life Technologies) using the EnTurbo™ SYBR Green PCR SuperMix kit (ELK Biotechnology, EQ001). Gene expression was quantified through the 2 − ΔΔCt method, with GAPDH serving as the reference gene in the experiments. The human primer sequences for all target genes are detailed in Table 2 . Chondrocytes underwent dual washing with chilled phosphate-buffered saline (ASPEN, AS1025) prior to lysis with protease inhibitor cocktail-containing RIPA lysis buffer (ASPEN, AS1004). Sample protein concentrations were evaluated using the BCA protein quantification kit (ASPEN, AS1086). Subsequently, protein samples (40 μg per lane) were taken and mixed with 5× protein loading buffer (ASPEN, AS1011) at the recommended ratio. The samples underwent heat denaturation (95 °C, 5 min) before electrophoretic separation on 10% SDS-PAGE (ASPEN, AS1012). Protein transfer was performed using PVDF membranes (Millipore, IPVH00010), followed by membrane blocking with 5% skim milk (ASPEN, AS1033) at room temperature for 1 h. After discarding the blocking solution, membranes were probed with primary antibody at 4 °C overnight, then treated with secondary antibody (30 min, room temperature) the next day. Finally, the protein bands were visualized and recorded using the ChemiScope 6000 chemiluminescence imaging system. The optical density of target bands was determined using AlphaEaseFC software. More details were presented in the Supplementary Material 1 .

R software (version 4.4.2) was employed for data processing. Intergroup differences were evaluated via the Wilcoxon test. In vitro experimental data were analyzed via a paired two-tailed t-test. Data results were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). A p value below 0.05 indicated statistical significance.

After batch effect removal from the training set (Fig. 1 A, B), 323 DEGs were identified. Among these, 217 genes were upregulated and 106 genes were downregulated (Fig. 1 C). The top 50 genes with the most significant expression differences in both upregulated and downregulated genes were then selected to create a heatmap visualization matrix (Fig. 1 D). Finally, the intersection of DEGs and 919 PMGs yielded 30 DEPMGs (Supplementary Material 2 ). Fig. 1 DEGs analysis. DEGs analysis. A Boxplots prior to batch correction; B Boxplots following batch correction; C Volcano plot of DEGs; D Heatmap representing the top 50 upregulated and downregulated genes

PPI network analysis was performed on the 30 DEPMGs utilizing information from the STRING database (Fig. 2 ). This analysis presented the interaction relationships between the 27 hub genes that are significantly involved in OA development. KEGG and GO analyses were performed to further investigate the molecular functions and signaling pathways of these genes (Fig. 3 ). GO enrichment analysis revealed that DEPMGs were primarily enriched in regulatory processes, including ‘cellular response to lipopolysaccharide’ and ‘cartilage development’, at the BP level. Regarding CC, these genes were significantly enriched in structures including ‘extracellular space’ and ‘extracellular exosome’. Regarding MF, DEPMGs were prominent in activity-related functions such as ‘peptidase activity’ and ‘enzyme binding’. The KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that DEPMGs exhibited significant enrichment characteristics in key signaling pathways, particularly PI3K-Akt and IL-17 cascades. These findings provide important clues for revealing OA’s pathogenesis. Fig. 2 PPI network analysis of DEPMGs

The merged training set was selected for WGCNA analysis. First, the initial sample cluster analysis (Fig. 4 A) revealed no outliers. Additionally, a soft threshold of β = 5 was applied to construct a scale-free network and ensure high connectivity (Fig. 4 B). Subsequently, according to the gene clustering tree and dynamic tree cutting algorithm, modules with high similarity were merged (Fig. 4 C). Next, eight gene co-expression modules most closely related to OA were identified (Fig. 4 D). Ultimately, modules significantly correlated with OA (|r|> 0.5, p < 0.05) were selected for downstream analysis. This identified the green module (r = 0.82, p = 1 × 10 −19 ) and the black module (r = 0.56, p = 2 × 10 −7 ), which together encompassed 381 genes and exhibited high variance explanation rates (Fig. 4 E). By analyzing the intersection of joint module genes and DEPMGs, 15 genes were finally screened out (Fig. 4 F). A correlation triangular heatmap was drawn via the qcorrplot package to visualize the expression correlation between the 15 genes (Fig. 4 G). The analysis revealed that certain gene pairs (e.g., SPP1 and PLOD1, COL6A1 and TSPO) demonstrated significant positive correlations, while other gene pairs (e.g., ATN1 and PLOD1) exhibited significant negative correlations. These results revealed potential functional associations between genes, possibly suggesting synergistic or antagonistic effects in biological processes.

To screen PM-related OA characteristic genes, the 15 candidate genes were applied to four commonly used machine learning algorithms (MLAs). First, LASSO regression was employed to identify 11 genes that could serve as diagnostic markers for OA (Fig. 5 A, B). The SVM-RFE algorithm screened out 7 important biomarkers (Fig. 5 C). Subsequently, RF technology was adopted to identify 11 genes as key biomarkers (Fig. 5 D, E). Meanwhile, 14 major biomarkers were screened based on the logistic regression algorithm (Fig. 5 F). Finally, the Venn diagram intersection yielded four hub genes: PLOD1, TSPO, SPP1, and COL6A1 (Fig. 5 G). Fig. 5 Machine learning. To improve the accuracy of OA prediction, a nomogram model containing four hub genes was established (Fig. 6 A). The calibration curve (Fig. 6 B) revealed minimal error between the predicted and actual disease risk, confirming the nomogram's high prediction accuracy for disease samples. DCA (Fig. 6 C) indicated that, although the model curve deviated from the curves, the model was accurate. ROC curve analysis showed that all four key genes had robust single-gene diagnostic performance in the training set. The respective AUC values were 0.899, 0.883, 0.875, and 0.813 for PLOD1, TSPO, SPP1, and COL6A1, respectively (Fig. 6 D–G). Integrating all four genes into a combined model improved performance further, with the original AUC reaching 0.967 and the Bootstrap-verified AUC being 0.948 (95% CI 0.925–0.975) (Fig. 7 A). In the external validation cohort, the single-gene AUCs ranged from 0.63 to 0.82, with COL6A1 maintaining an excellent level of 0.82 (Fig. 6 H–K). The four-gene combined model also performed well with an AUC of 0.95 (Fig. 7 B). Furthermore, box plot analysis revealed that in the diagnostic set, all four marker genes demonstrated significant overexpression in OA individuals compared to controls (Fig. 6 L–O). Differences in immune cell infiltration between the OA group and the normal group were compared through box plots (Fig. 8 A, B). Six types of immune cells were found to differ significantly. Specifically, M0 and M2 macrophages and gamma delta T cells were significantly enriched in the OA group. Dendritic cells (activated and resting) and NK cells (activated) were mainly enriched in the normal group. Spearman correlation analysis was conducted to explore the intrinsic association between hub genes and immune cell infiltration (Fig. 8 C). The results showed that all core genes were positively correlated with M0 macrophages. Further correlation analysis for immune checkpoint gene expression and immune cell abundance revealed that diagnostic genes were significantly positively linked to CD44 and significantly negatively linked to TNFSF14 (Fig. 8 D). These results indicate that the immune microenvironment of OA patients is significantly altered, suggesting that these characteristic genes have a potential role in regulating disease-related immune responses. To explore the transcription factors (TFs) and miRNAs that may regulate key genes, TF and miRNA data were analyzed. The TF-gene network consisted of 29 nodes and 31 edges (Fig. 9 A). TFs, such as PELA, KLF5, FOXF2, FOXL1, NFKB1, and ZNF354C, could serve as pivotal regulators of hub gene networks. Based on the mirTarbase database, a gene-miRNA interaction network was analyzed (Fig. 9 B). This analysis revealed a network in which the two core genes, COL6A1 and SPP1, acted as hubs, connecting 11 miRNA molecules. Notably, both COL6A1 and SPP1 were regulated by hsa-mir-335-5p. Another network demonstrated that PLOD1 connected seven miRNAs. In summary, the expression of key genes may be subject to multilevel regulation by various TFs and miRNAs. Following CMap analysis of DEGs, ten compounds with the lowest scores were identified: ZG-10, chromomycin-a3, daunorubicin, ER-27319, triptolide, PIK-75, AT-7519, pidorubicine, alvocidib, and PF-562271 (Supplementary Material 3 ). A review of existing evidence related to OA revealed that most of these compounds have primarily been investigated in oncology or general cell signaling contexts [ 20 – 22 ]. This limits their direct relevance to OA pathogenesis and offers an insufficient basis for further exploration as potential OA therapeutics. Notably, triptolide is an exception. It exerts anti-inflammatory effects on chondrocytes by inhibiting NLRP3 inflammasome activation and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production. This may occur via suppression of the Wnt/β-catenin and NF-κB pathways [ 23 , 24 ]. Furthermore, research by Li et al. demonstrated that triptolide downregulated the expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) 3 and 13, thereby attenuating cartilage matrix degradation [ 25 , 26 ]. Triptolide’s combined anti-inflammatory and chondroprotective properties suggest its potential as a novel OA therapeutic candidate. Subsequent molecular docking was performed to evaluate the binding affinity between triptolide and four candidate targets. The calculated binding energies for triptolide with PLOD1, SPP1, TSPO, and COL6A1 were − 9.3, − 8.8, − 7.7, and − 7.2 kcal/mol, respectively (Fig. 10 A–D). All values are below − 5 kcal/mol, indicating that triptolide exhibits high binding affinity toward each target, with the strongest interaction observed for PLOD1. Fig. 10 Molecular docking. To further investigate the stability of the PLOD1-triptolide complex, a 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation was conducted. The average RMSD value for the PLOD1-triptolide complex was 2.11 ± 0.39 Å, indicating relatively stable protein-small molecule binding with minimal deviation throughout the simulation (Fig. 11 A). The Rg value of the PLOD1-triptolide complex was determined to be 35.27 ± 0.19 Å, reflecting its compact structure (Fig. 11 B). Additionally, the SASA of the PLOD1-triptolide complex exhibited excellent stability at 32,037.70 ± 381.09 Å 2 (Fig. 11 C). The hydrogen bonds formed within the complex remained stable, averaging one to two bonds (Fig. 11 D). The RMSF analysis yielded a value of 2.08 ± 0.43 Å, suggesting that ligand binding did not significantly impact the protein's flexibility (Fig. 11 E). Overall, the PLOD1-triptolide complex exhibits stable binding with well-developed hydrogen bonding interactions. Fig. 11 Molecular dynamics simulation. To verify the expression of diagnostic genes in an OA chondrocyte model, qRT-PCR and Western blot experiments were further conducted. sections.discussion:
OA constitutes a prevalent, progressive, and disabling joint disorder that affects middle-aged and older populations [ 3 ]. Traditional diagnosis relies primarily on clinical symptoms and imaging evaluations. However, these methods have low sensitivity for early OA. They often fail to detect micro-damage to cartilage and early inflammatory responses in time, thus missing the optimal window for intervention. In recent years, research has increasingly demonstrated that PM is strongly linked to the onset and progression of diseases like OA. PM is a complex biological process that plays an important role in cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, and maintaining cell homeostasis [ 27 , 28 ]. PAs have been reported to regulate the intracellular oxidative balance and the inflammatory response, protect chondrocytes from oxidative damage, and promote chondrocyte production [ 16 ]. However, the relationship between PM and OA and its specific mechanisms remain unclear. Thus, the current study aims to explore the differential gene expression patterns related to PM in OA and to investigate potential related signaling pathways to identify potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

GO and KEGG analyses revealed that 30 DEPMGs were closely related to biological processes such as ‘cellular response to lipopolysaccharide’, ‘cartilage development’, ‘extracellular space’, ‘enzyme binding’, and ‘IL-17 signaling pathway’. Existing evidence strongly supports the association of these pathways with the pathological process of OA. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is a classic activator of the innate immune system [ 29 ]. Research has found that LPS can induce the elevated expression of TLR4 in chondrocytes , activate the NF-κB pathway, and promote the release of inflammatory mediators [ 30 , 31 ]. It also increases the expression of matrix-degrading enzymes, leading to extracellular-matrix breakdown and accelerated cartilage degeneration [ 30 ]. Furthermore, aging and OA cartilage exhibit reduced PA synthesis, which decreases the expression of acetyltransferase EP300 [ 17 ]. This leads to decreased acetylation modification levels of key autophagy proteins LC3 and Beclin1, decreased cartilage autophagy activity, and accelerated cartilage degeneration [ 32 , 33 ]. PM can regulate the immune function of γδ T cells by modulating cytokine secretion. γδ T cells promote synovial inflammation by secreting cytokines such as IL-17 [ 34 , 35 ]. Further analysis revealed that IL-17 creates a vicious cycle by regulating chondrocyte autophagy, senescence, and cartilage matrix degradation [ 34 , 36 ]. Analyzing the functions and pathways of DEPMGs provided deeper insight into the pathophysiological processes associated with OA.

PLOD1 is a key gene that regulates lysine hydroxylation [ 37 ]. It is essential for collagen cross-linking and deposition [ 37 ]. In OA, changes in PM may affect intracellular S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) levels [ 38 ]. SAM is an indispensable methyl donor in the DNA methylation process. Increased SAM levels can enhance the activity of DNA methyltransferases, thereby affecting the methylation state of genes [ 39 , 40 ]. This may be one of the mechanisms leading to PLOD1 gene upregulation. PLOD1 upregulation can result in excessive collagen synthesis and cross-linking. These changes lead to cartilage matrix hardening, reduced elasticity, and decreased compressive strength [ 41 ]. This increases the risk of cartilage damage under mechanical stress and may exacerbate inflammation and cartilage injury [ 42 ]. TSPO is a protein located on the outer mitochondrial membrane [ 43 ]. In OA synovial tissue, TSPO expression shows an increasing trend, consistent with the research results of Palada et al. [ 44 ]. TSPO activation triggers the NF-κB signaling pathway, which promotes M1 macrophage polarization and the release of proinflammatory cytokines [ 45 ]. Recent studies have demonstrated the promising potential of using TSPO as a positron emission tomography (PET) imaging marker to characterize the inflammatory subtype of OA and to monitor treatment responses [ 46 ]. SPP1 encodes osteopontin (OPN), a highly phosphorylated and glycosylated protein [ 47 , 48 ]. Numerous studies have shown that OA is associated with elevated OPN expression levels in synovial membranes and cartilage [ 49 , 50 ]. OPN accelerates chondrocyte proliferation by promoting NF-κB signaling during the pathological process of OA , thereby inducing OA onset in rat models [ 51 ]. OPN also inhibits autophagy via the CD44/MAPK pathway [ 52 ]. Furthermore, research suggests that OPN may significantly impact the destruction of articular cartilage by promoting synovial angiogenesis and inducing chondrocyte apoptosis [ 53 ]. COL6A1 encodes the α1 chain of type VI collagen, a key element of the extracellular matrix [ 54 ]. COL6A1 serves as a critical component in preserving tissue architecture and physiological function, including cell adhesion, migration, and tissue mechanical strength [ 55 ]. Studies suggest that elevated COL6A1 expression is associated with subchondral bone remodeling and may worsen OA progression by promoting osteoclast differentiation and formation via the EPAC/RAP1 signaling axis [ 54 , 55 ]. These key genes provide new evidence for the future diagnosis of OA. The research results also enrich the lineage of OA diagnostic biomarkers. These four hub genes can serve as new reference molecules for future OA diagnostic research. However, continuous efforts are required for in-depth verification in subsequent studies.

Immune-inflammatory response is the core link in the pathogenesis and progression of OA. Damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) released by damaged cartilage and bone matrix can rapidly activate the crosstalk between innate and adaptive immunity, converting initial mechanical injury signals into a self-sustaining and self-amplifying chronic immune-inflammatory cycle, which exacerbates joint structural destruction [ 56 ]. Immune cell infiltration analysis of OA tissues using the CIBERSORT algorithm revealed a significant enrichment of Macrophages M0, Macrophages M2, and gamma delta T cells [ 57 , 58 ]. Among them, M0 macrophages can polarize into M1 or M2 subtypes under the stimulation of the local joint microenvironment: the M1 subtype tends to secrete pro-inflammatory factors to aggravate inflammatory damage, while the M2 subtype can inhibit inflammatory responses and participate in tissue repair [ 58 ]. A study by Blom et al. found that synovial macrophages can mediate osteophyte formation in OA [ 59 ]. After selective depletion of synovial macrophages, researchers observed a reduction in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, osteophyte formation, and cartilage destruction [ 60 , 61 ]. This suggests that macrophage depletion may serve as a potential therapeutic intervention for OA [ 62 ]. In addition, gamma delta T cells are characterized by their unique cytotoxic and immunomodulatory functions, playing important roles in both innate and adaptive immune responses [ 63 ]. Notably, CIBERSORT achieves the highest accuracy in immune-dominant tissues such as blood and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. In avascular cartilage and synovium where infiltration changes dramatically with disease progression, its quantitative results may show systematic bias and should be interpreted with caution.

This study has the following limitations. First, all bioinformatics data used in this study were sourced from public databases. Not only is the sample size limited, but the data quality cannot be fully controlled, which may introduce potential biases and impose restrictions on the study results. Second, validation experiments were only conducted in single-cell models and have not yet undergone cross-validation using human tissues, multiple arthritis animal models, or different cell lines, resulting in insufficient extrapolation of the study conclusions. Future research should establish prospective clinical cohorts and combine more in-depth in vitro and in vivo molecular biology experiments to systematically verify the role of these genes in the occurrence and development of OA, thereby identifying potential therapeutic targets. Before obtaining more confirmatory evidence, the general applicability and clinical relevance of the conclusions of this study remain exploratory.
sections.conclusion: In this study, we initially screened 4 hub PMGs (PLOD1, TSPO, SPP1, and COL6A1) using machine learning and found that they play an important role in OA. Further molecular docking and dynamics simulations suggested that triptolide may have therapeutic potential against OA. These findings provide valuable insights for diagnostic research on OA and the development of new therapeutic strategies. Future efforts should validate the roles of these genes in larger populations and further explore their therapeutic potential to gain a more comprehensive understanding.
